どう おもいます か — What do you think?
You give your opinion (～と おもいます), report what someone else said (～と いいました) and make guesses (～でしょう), using the casual form inside the sentence.
I think, it seems to me (→ おもう)
I pass on (a message) (→ つたえる)
long ago, in the old days
all the time; for a long time
I think it will rain tomorrow.
To give your opinion: [casual form] + と おもいます.
To ask someone’s opinion: ～に ついて どう おもいます か.
To report someone’s words: directly (「…」と いいました) and indirectly (… と いいました).
To make guesses: ～でしょう, たぶん, きっと.
To use the casual form INSIDE a polite sentence.
In Kyoto, Mihai finally opened Mrs Suzuki’s bag. The letter was for her younger sister, Fumiko, who runs a tea house near a temple. Mihai and Ana find her.
Yes. Er, are you Mrs Suzuki Fumiko?
We’ve been asked to bring you a letter from Mrs Suzuki Michiko in Madrid.
…From my sister? We haven’t spoken for fifty years.
My sister married a Spaniard. Our father was against it. And I told her: “Don’t go.”
But she went. Since then, the two of us have always…
Mrs Michiko is always talking about Kyoto. I think she must be lonely.
Yes, she’s well. She works at the library. She looks after a cat too.
She said José passed away last year.
I see… (She reads the letter) …“Fumiko, forgive me. I want to see you.”
Mrs Fumiko, what do you think?
…I think I’m the one who should apologise. Father is gone now too. There’s probably nobody left to object.
Excuse me, could you give me her phone number?
Of course. I think Mrs Michiko will be overjoyed.
talk (“no hanashi o suru” = talks about)
care (“sewa o suru” = to look after)
passed away (casual form, polite in meaning)
“oshiete itadakemasen ka” = could you tell me? (very polite)
Run it together: “to omoimas”. Your voice falls at the end: it’s a statement, not a question.
“deshoh”, with a long o. With a falling voice = “probably”. With a rising voice = “isn’t it?”.
go-men-na-sai: ん is a whole beat. It’s a sincere apology, more personal than すみません.
1. Your opinion: [casual] + と おもいます
An opinion has two parts: WHAT you think (in the CASUAL form, from chapter 17) + と おもいます (I think). と is the Japanese “quotation mark”: it marks the content of the thought.
With と おもいます
あめ が ふる と おもいます (I think it will rain)
こない と おもいます (I don’t think he’ll come)
しずか だ と おもいます ⚠️ だ is required!
The classic mistake: “たかい です と おもいます”. です does NOT go inside! Inside it’s always the casual form.
With な adjectives and nouns, だ is required before と: きれい だ と おもいます (not “きれい と おもいます”).
What do you think about Japanese food?
To agree / disagree: X に さんせい です / X に はんたい です.
Japanese people use と おもいます MUCH more often than English speakers say “I think”. They like to soften their statements. “It’s expensive” can sound blunt; “たかい と おもいます” sounds more modest.
3. What someone said: と いいました
the exact words in 「 」 + と いいました
casual form + と いいました
Japanese quotation marks look like this: 「 … 」. You’ve seen them in all the stories!
The teacher said there’s a test tomorrow.
For “X is called…” use the same structure: これ は にほんご で「さくら」と いいます (In Japanese this is called “sakura”).
4. Guesses: でしょう, たぶん, きっと
でしょう comes after the casual form (without だ!) and means “probably”. It’s often accompanied by an adverb showing how sure you are:
It will probably be clear tomorrow.
Mrs Michiko will definitely be happy.
With な adjectives and nouns, だ disappears before でしょう: しずか でしょう (not “しずか だ でしょう”).
With rising intonation, でしょう? (or casual でしょ?) means “isn’t it?”. Sakura said “でしょ?” at Miyajima!
5. Review: the casual form inside sentences
You’ve seen the casual form in lots of places. They all follow the same rule: inside it’s casual, and the politeness comes only AT THE END.
～た こと が あります (ch. 16)
Now you understand why you learned the casual forms: they’re the “bricks” complex sentences are built with.
What do you think about Kyoto?
I think Mrs Michiko will be happy.
How long have the sisters not spoken?
What did Fumiko say to her sister back then?
Who does Fumiko think should apologise?
What does Fumiko ask for at the end?
きょうと の いんしょう — Impressions of Kyoto
Ana writes on the club blog what she thinks of Kyoto, after three days there.
I think Kyoto is completely different from Tokyo.
Tokyo is a new, fast city. But in Kyoto I think time flows slowly.
Yuki said: “Kyoto is most beautiful in autumn.” It was true!
The maples were red and yellow, and the temple gardens looked like paintings.
But there are a great many tourists. I thought it was rather noisy at midday.
Mihai keeps saying: “I want to live in Kyoto.” He’s probably joking.
Tomorrow we go back to Hiroshima. I’m happy when I think I’ll see Sakura again.
to be able to see again

ふたり の しまい — The two sisters
That evening, Mihai and Ana stayed on at Mrs Fumiko’s tea house.
The tea house was already closed. A single small light was burning in the garden.
Mrs Fumiko was holding the phone and didn’t move for a long time.
“I don’t know what to say. Fifty years is too long.”
Ana sat down next to Mrs Fumiko.
“Mrs Michiko thinks you’re angry with her. That’s why she couldn’t call for so long.”
“Then tell her that. I think that’s enough.”
In Madrid it’s twelve noon now. The time difference is eight hours.
“Mrs Michiko is probably at the library now,” said Mihai.
Mrs Fumiko took a deep breath and dialled the number.
Mrs Fumiko’s lips trembled. No sound would come out.
There was silence at the other end.
Then the two of them cried, laughed, and so on.
Mihai and Ana slipped quietly out into the garden.
Because they thought it wasn’t right to listen to their conversation.
The garden was quiet. The maple leaves looked black in the moonlight.
“Mihai, do you think it was chance that you found Mrs Suzuki’s photo?”
“I don’t know. But I want to believe it wasn’t chance.”
Mihai touched the lucky charm in his pocket.
He remembered the words on the fortune slip from Asakusa: “The important person is already close.”
Just then the tea-house door opened.
Mrs Fumiko came out. Her eyes were red, but her face was bright.
“My sister said she’s coming to Kyoto in the spring next year. She says she wants us to see the cherry blossoms together.”
“Thank you from the bottom of my heart. You two are our guardian angels.”
Mrs Fumiko made them a hot cup of tea.
“This is my sister’s favourite tea. Long ago we often drank it together.”
Mrs Fumiko gave Ana a small box.
“Please take this to my sister. I think she’ll definitely be happy.”
On the way back, Mihai never managed to finish the sentence “I…”.
But Ana had probably already understood.
After getting back to the hotel, Ana sent Yuki a message.
“Today the two sisters spoke for the first time in fifty years. Our letter became a bridge between them.”
The answer came straight away. “Amazing! Mrs Suzuki cried all day at the library today. But she looked very happy.”
“And Tama slept on Mrs Suzuki’s lap all day.”
Ana smiled and looked out of the window at the Kyoto night. Tomorrow they’re going to Hiroshima.
“ieba ii ka” = what I should say
I missed her, I was lonely
“kiite wa ikenai” = it isn’t right to listen

She thought Fumiko was angry with her

So as not to listen to the sisters’ conversation
